etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English profound, from Anglo-Norman profound, from Old French profont, from Latin profundus, from pro + fundus (“bottom; foundation”).

definitions.definition: Descending far below the surface; opening or reaching to great depth; deep.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “(please specify the page number)”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: A gulf profound as that Serbonian bog

definitions.definition: Intellectually deep; entering far into subjects; reaching to the bottom of a matter, or of a branch of learning; thorough

quote.citation: 1819, Washington Irving, The Sketch Book, English Writers on America:
quote.text: Where no motives of interest or pride intervene, none can equal them for profound and philosophical views of society, ….

definitions.definition: Characterized by intensity; deeply felt; pervading

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Measure for Measure”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: How now! which of your hips has the most profound sciatica?

quote.citation: 1860, Henry Hart Milman, History of Latin Christianity : including that of the popes to the pontificate of Nicholas V.:
quote.text: Of the profound corruption of this class there can be no doubt.

quote.citation: 2019, Shelina Janmohamed, “Long before Shamima Begum, Muslim women were targets”, in Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: It’s probably one of the reasons the Shamima Begum case is having such a profound impact; one-dimensional stereotypes about Muslim women already run so deep.

quote.citation: 2023 September 20, Nigel Harris, “Comment Special: And it's goodbye from me...”, in RAIL, number 992, page 3:
quote.text: I visited the wreckage at Ladbroke Grove, Hatfield. Potters Bar and Heck, and the experiences had a profound effect on me - especially Ladbroke Grove.

definitions.definition: Bending low, exhibiting or expressing deep humility; lowly; submissive

quote.citation: 1847 January – 1848 July, William Makepeace Thackeray, Vanity Fair […], London: Bradbury and Evans […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: And with this, and a profound bow to his patrons, the Manager retires, and the curtain rises.

quote.citation: a. 1662, Brian Duppa, Holy Rules and Helps to Devotion, published 1683:
quote.text: What humble gestures! What profound reverence!

definitions.definition: (obsolete) The deep; the sea; the ocean.

quote.citation: 1638, George Sandys, A Paraphrase vpon the Divine Poems, Exodvs 15:
quote.text: God, in the fathomlesse profound / Hath all his choice Commanders drown'd.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book II”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, lines 976-980:
quote.text: […] if some other place, / From your dominion won, th' Ethereal King / Possesses lately, thither to arrive / travel this profound. Direct my course […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To cause to sink deeply; to cause to dive or penetrate far down.

quote.citation: 1650, Thomas Browne, Pseudodoxia Epidemica: […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  A[braham] Miller, for Edw[ard] Dod and Nath[aniel] Ekins, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: But no man is likely to profound tbe Ocean of that Doctrine
